answer.label: Not Leonardo da Vinci — actually Barry Commoner
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Leonardo da Vinci ever wrote this line, and none of his notebooks contain it. As a stated maxim the exact wording is the first of biologist Barry Commoner’s four “laws of ecology” in The Closing Circle (1971). Related thoughts appear earlier in Lessing (1769), Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. (1896) and John Muir (1911), per Quote Investigator ↗.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from
source.excerpt: Everything is connected to everything else.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the earliest da Vinci attribution only to a 1991 newspaper and finds that “this evidence is not substantive” — read the investigation ↗.
The exact wording is documented as the first of Barry Commoner’s four laws of ecology in The Closing Circle (1971), per Wikipedia ↗.
Earlier kindred lines include John Muir’s 1911 “When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the Universe,” noted by Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: The first of Barry Commoner’s four “laws of ecology” in The Closing Circle (1971); the remaining three are “Everything must go somewhere,” “Nature knows best,” and “There is no such thing as a free lunch.”

source.rightsNote: The best-documented source of this exact wording, Barry Commoner’s The Closing Circle, was first published in 1971 and remains in copyright in the United States. The line is not tied to any pre-1931 work of Leonardo da Vinci, so no public-domain status can be claimed for this phrasing.

author.name: Barry Commoner
author.heading: About Barry Commoner
author.bio: Barry Commoner was an American cellular biologist who became one of the founders of the modern environmental movement. In his 1971 bestseller The Closing Circle he distilled ecological thinking into four memorable “laws,” the first being “everything is connected to everything else.” He ran for U.S. president in 1980 on the Citizens Party ticket.

misattribution.heading: How Leonardo got the credit
misattribution.intro: This tidy, holistic-sounding line is exactly the kind of aphorism that gets pinned on Leonardo da Vinci — a byword for genius who conveniently died in 1519 and cannot object.

items.scope: Everything is connected to everything else
items.why: No Leonardo notebook or letter contains this line. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the earliest da Vinci attribution only in a 1991 newspaper — nearly five centuries after his death.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is old and the wording is Barry Commoner’s (1971); the Leonardo label is a late-20th-century invention with no support ↗.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The line reads like ancient wisdom, but its modern fame is ecological. Barry Commoner used it in 1971 to argue that you cannot tinker with one part of an ecosystem without consequences rippling everywhere — a rebuke to reductionist, pollute-and-forget thinking.

Because the idea feels timeless, it drifted onto Renaissance-genius quote lists. Leonardo did write admiringly about the interconnection of natural forms, which makes the misattribution feel plausible — but feeling plausible is not the same as being sourced.
context.pull: Old idea, modern wording — and not Leonardo’s.
